item.title: Federal agents search Rep. Ilhan Omar's home weeks before the midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rep. Ilhan Omar takes questions during a news conference at the Capitol in Washington on January 13, 2026. - J. Scott Applewhite/AP/File Federal officers executed a search warrant early Monday at the Washington, DC-area home of Rep. Ilhan Omar , the Minnesota Democrat who has been the persistent target of ire from President Donald Trump’s administration, according to a Justice Department spokesperson and a source familiar with the matter. The congresswoman is running for reelection and the search warrant was executed only weeks before the midterms. It is unusual for the Justice Department to take such an aggressive investigative step toward a candidate so close to an election. Voting is well underway in Minnesota, with more than 127,000 people having already voted, according to data from the secretary of state. The Department of Justice said in a statement Monday that investigators from Homeland Security Investigations, a branch of the Department of Homeland Security that handles criminal investigations, “executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice.” “This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal criminal investigation,” a DOJ spokesperson said. The statement did not indicate what the investigation entailed. Omar called the search “the latest escalation” in Trump’s “campaign of political intimidation.” “I’m ok. Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement,” she wrote on X . “For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns. This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced.” Homeland Security Investigations agents work outside the Washington, DC, residence of Rep. Ilhan Omar on Monday. - Annabelle Gordon/Reuters Later on Monday, Trump called Omar “a terrible person,” but insisted he was not involved in the search of her home. “I understand they’re looking at her very carefully – I’ve always found her to be a totally crooked person,” the president told reporters at the White House, adding the search on Monday “has nothing to do with me.” “I think she’s a terrible person, but that’s really up to the DOJ, I have nothing to do with it,” he said. House Democratic leaders called the search “deeply disturbing” and said it “raises serious questions about the continued corrupt weaponization of the federal government against Donald Trump’s adversaries.” “For years, Donald Trump and far-right extremists have relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Omar with vile personal attacks and baseless accusations,” House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, Whip Katherine Clark and caucus Chair Pete Aguilar said in a statement, adding that it comes with “less than 30 days until the midterm election.” A spokesperson for the congresswoman said in a statement to CNN, “For a decade, Donald Trump has relentlessly targeted Congresswoman Ilhan Omar with inflammatory rhetoric, repeatedly putting a target on her back … The Congresswoman has done nothing wrong.” unknown content item - While authorities have not said what prompted the search, administration officials have previously indicated that Omar was facing an investigation. White House border czar Tom Homan said on Fox News last month that “things are going on” in relation to Omar, before adding: “But I can’t give the specifics of what’s happening.” Speaking to Fox on Monday morning, Homan confirmed the search warrant was executed, but provided no other information. “The specifics of the investigation, I think I need to turn that over to Todd Blanche or Markwayne Mullin,” he said, referring to the attorney general and DHS secretary. “I don’t want to get ahead of them commenting on an ongoing investigation.” One of Omar’s neighbors told CNN they were awoken around 4:30 a.m. Monday to the sounds of banging on doors. Later that morning, CNN observed that the home was surrounded by Homeland Security Investigations officers and that investigators were removing boxes from the home. Before leaving the scene, officials used a camera to document the condition of the house. Omar was born in Somalia and grew up at the peak of that country’s civil war. She fled to the US as a teenager and later became a US citizen. She was first elected to Congress in 2018 and became part of “ The Squad ,” a group of congresswomen of color known for pushing for progressive causes. Since joining Congress, she has been the target of racist vitriol, including from Trump, who called Omar “garbage” last year and said Somalis should “go back to where they came from.” Omar’s home district in Minnesota was the target of an expansive immigration-enforcement campaign earlier this year that led to violent clashes between protesters and immigration authorities and the fatal shootings of two US citizens. Top administration officials, including Homeland Security Secretary Mullin, have accused Omar of marrying her brother to help bring him into the United States. They have provided no proof of this claim. Homan said on Fox News last month, referencing Omar, that if “someone committed immigration violation, someone committed marriage fraud, or anything like that, regardless if they’re a congressman or not, no one’s above the law.” Homeland Security Investigations officers carry boxes Rep. Ilhan Omar's residence. - J. Scott Applewhite/AP Asked specifically whether that means there was an open investigation into Omar, Homan responded: “I’m confirming that ICE is — yeah, like I said months ago, that is something that’s been reported and needs to be looked at.” In prior years, the department has treaded cautiously for the 60-day period before an Election Day to not make searches or levy charges that would disadvantage a candidate. Department policy also bars prosecutors and investigative agents from selecting timing in an investigation so that it would influence an election. Top Justice Department leadership signed off on the search after thorough deliberations given the proximity to the election, and a federal judge ultimately approved it, a source familiar with the investigation told CNN on Monday. The Justice Department also has special policies requiring additional approvals when investigations involve a member of Congress, and the Constitution provides additional protections for members around papers and communications that relate to their legislative work. This story has been updated with additional information. CNN’s Kristen Holmes, Annie Grayer, Donald Judd and Nick Leimbach contributed to this report. For more CNN news and newsletters create an account at CNN.com This article originally appeared on CNN at https://www.cnn.com/2026/10/12/politics/ilhan-omar-search

item.title: 'We are on a rowboat': Inside the Army's push to catch up on drone warfare
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
( NewsNation ) — Fort Polk in western Louisiana is where soldiers go to “play war.” It’s home to the Joint Readiness Training Center (JRTC), where troops prepare for combat, especially before deploying. The goal of the Army's combat training centers is to replicate real-world warfare, and that increasingly means preparing for conflict shaped by drones and artificial intelligence. Bryan Pickens, a veteran who served 14 combat deployments to Afghanistan and Iraq and has more than 20 years of military service in U.S. Special Operations, said the United States has a lot of catching up to do. “I often say we are on a rowboat while our enemies are escaping us on a jet ski,” Pickens said. “The Global War on Terror skills prepared us to fight dirt farmers. Not our peer enemies.” Pentagon clears way for anti-drone tech: Hegseth memo Having also supported Ukraine’s current war effort against Russia , Pickens now focuses on training U.S. and NATO forces on current warfare and modernizing the force. The Pentagon announced a new Autonomous Warfare Command, led by a four-star general to scale AI, robotics and low-cost drone capabilities across the military. NewsNation has learned exclusively that another goal of that push is the launch of an integrated technology system for the Army that works across equipment from different manufacturers and is designed to speed up training and cut costs. The first testing ground for this is the JRTC in partnership with Forterra, a defense tech company focused on autonomous ground systems that is now expanding how they can serve the U.S. military. Empowering the 'bad guys' to help the 'good guys' get better To simulate realistic combat, the 1st Battalion, 509th Infantry Regiment, nicknamed Geronimo, serves as the resident opposing force and plays the enemy against every brigade that rotates through the training center. Soldiers in Geronimo are given tools that mimic what enemies of the U.S. have or are expected to have, including drones, communications and intelligence information, said Logan Morris, chairman of Fort Polk Progress. Morris is also a former civilian aide to the secretary of the Army. Dealing with a variety of autonomous enemy weapons systems, whether they’re coming from Russia , Iran, China or elsewhere, means the military needs different technologies that run on individual platforms. Soldiers then must learn how to use each platform and process the data separately before it all gets integrated, something that takes time and money. Pentagon may increase unmanned canoe-size drones on the Rio Grande The new system aims to reduce both. Phil Cotter, Forterra’s head of growth, sustainment and shaping operations, said, “What Geronimo is good at is flummoxing these units that come down [to Fort Polk]. They shouldn't have to also be burdened with trying to learn 50 different systems, 50 different battery chargers, 50 different handheld controllers and range limitations” to successfully recreate what the enemy may do. The platform, known as OASIS-Fabric and OneLink, pulls in information from a range of communications technologies and other platforms and processes it at scale. Cotter explains, “They are the middleware and data layer that kind of allow these systems to all speak the same language.” Scott Sanders, Forterra's chief growth officer, said the goal is for a tired, stressed 18-year-old on the battlefield to be able to plan a mission without waiting on higher headquarters. The soldier “should be able to do all the mission autonomy planning right there without having to reach back to higher headquarters to do it … you can reduce cost, enhance interoperability, and increase the speed at which decisions get made at tactical edge," he said. Meet the AI-piloted fighter jet being built in the US Morris explains the goal is not just to give this capability to Geronimo but also to those battalions who go down to train, aka the “good guys.” He said it stands out because it "integrates and evaluates capabilities from other companies, vendors and contractors,” rather than interfering with each other. That would let other defense companies' platforms work together as one larger system. If the system proves successful, the plan is to bring it to all of the Army's training centers and eventually to combat operations. Army needs transformation ASAP, warns commander Lt. Col. Trevor Jones, commander of Geronimo, wrote the Army needs to change how it trains and fights, learning what works and what doesn’t by “failing fast.” “The risk of being outclassed by a rival military’s transformation is very real with the current pace of technological change," Jones said. Forterra acknowledges there’s no guarantee this new platform will work perfectly, and certainly not right away. But Jones’ argument for experimentation is that if the U.S. military doesn’t try new ways of operating, it will fall even farther behind its enemies who are innovating in this space and have a headstart. Hegseth invites governors to bid for 'next great American base' This new technology has been tested to some degree. In the past year, Forterra has sent 105 autonomous vehicles to Eastern Europe to facilitate Ukraine’s fight . Cotter says some of the underlying technology used in those vehicles, and that’s been improved upon in battle, is some of the same tech that undergirds what Geronimo will be receiving. Sanders says they successfully tested out the system in Ukraine and because of that, “We said, ‘Let's roll this out broadly to the U.S. military, one training center at a time.’" Is the data coming into the platform secure? When asked how secure the data coming into their platform will be and whether there’s a risk for it to get in the hands of America’s enemies, Cotter says they are equipped to mitigate that because they’re “familiar with how to handle government data and not put any of that at risk to adversaries.” He points to the fact that Forterra has the first major ground autonomy program of record for the Department of War, which means it has already gone through an Authority to Operate process. Time will tell what gaps need to be filled and what other precautions need to be taken. For now, this platform appears to be a step toward warfare readiness. Congressman Mike Simpson, R-Idaho , says, “We can't let our adversaries get ahead of us, and they are ahead of us if we don't catch up real fast,” but he says he’s “excited that we can protect our war fighters” with new technology. item.title: Marijuana is on the ballot in 2026. The debate has changed.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Voters in Massachusetts, Idaho, and Houston are reconsidering marijuana legalization, who controls it, and how existing laws are enforced. getty Ten years after Massachusetts voters legalized recreational marijuana, they’re being asked to reverse course. Meanwhile, voters in Idaho and Houston will weigh in on who gets to decide marijuana policy and how existing laws should be enforced. The November 3 election offers an interesting snapshot of how the marijuana debate is changing. And for employers, the results could have implications for everything from workplace accommodations to drug testing and criminal background checks. Massachusetts: Could Legalization Go Into Reverse? Massachusetts voters approved recreational marijuana in 2016, and the industry has grown considerably since then. In September, the state’s Cannabis Control Commission reported that recreational marijuana businesses had surpassed $10 billion in cumulative sales . Now, voters are being asked whether to dismantle that market. Question 8 would eliminate recreational marijuana sales, the associated tax and regulatory framework, and home cultivation. Adults 21 and older could still possess up to one ounce, subject to limits on concentrates, without penalties. Medical marijuana would remain legal. If approved, the measure would take effect January 1, 2028. Massachusetts would become the first state to repeal a voter-approved recreational marijuana market. So, why reconsider legalization after a decade? Supporters point to concerns about youth access, impaired driving, mental health, and the commercialization of cannabis. They argue that the regulated market has brought consequences voters didn’t fully anticipate in 2016. Opponents warn that eliminating recreational sales could push consumers toward illicit markets, eliminate tax revenue, and threaten businesses and jobs. It’s a notable shift in a country where marijuana policy has generally moved toward greater legalization. Massachusetts could become a test of whether voters are willing to revisit an established cannabis market. For businesses operating in that market, the stakes are substantial. Recreational retailers, cultivators, and other operators could face significant disruption, although qualifying businesses could seek medical marijuana licenses. For other employers, the more immediate question is what happens to existing workplace protections. Massachusetts legalized medical marijuana in 2012, and its courts have recognized that employees using marijuana to treat qualifying medical conditions may be entitled to reasonable accommodation. In Barbuto v. Advantage Sales and Marketing , the state’s highest court considered a case involving an employee who was terminated after testing positive for marijuana despite disclosing her medical use. The court concluded that the employer could have an obligation to consider a reasonable accommodation under state disability discrimination law, even though marijuana remained illegal federally. Employers may still consider safety concerns, undue hardship, and applicable federal requirements. But they generally cannot dismiss an accommodation request simply because it involves medical marijuana. Because Question 8 would preserve medical marijuana, those considerations would remain relevant regardless of the election outcome. Idaho: Who Gets To Decide? While Massachusetts voters reconsider a legalization decision made a decade ago, Idaho voters will decide who gets to make that decision in the future. House Joint Resolution 4 would amend the state constitution to give the legislature exclusive authority to legalize marijuana, narcotics, and other psychoactive substances. Citizens could no longer use ballot initiatives to legalize those substances. Idaho currently prohibits both recreational and medical marijuana. Advocates have repeatedly attempted to place medical marijuana legalization before voters, including an initiative that failed to qualify for the 2026 ballot. Supporters of HJR 4 believe legalization decisions should go through the legislative process, where lawmakers can conduct hearings and evaluate proposed regulations. Opponents argue that the amendment would unnecessarily restrict voters’ ability to change state law. For employers, the immediate impact would be limited. Idaho’s marijuana prohibitions and existing workplace drug-testing requirements would remain unchanged. Under Idaho Code § 72-1705, employers seeking the protections of the state’s Employer Alcohol and Drug-Free Workplace Act generally must maintain a written testing policy. The policy must identify the types of testing conducted, be communicated to affected employees and available to applicants, and explain that violations may result in termination for misconduct. The statute also recognizes an exception for qualifying collectively bargained policies. Those requirements would remain in place regardless of the election outcome. The longer-term significance is how Idaho’s marijuana laws could evolve. In states where voters have approved legalization through ballot initiatives, those changes have sometimes prompted additional debates about drug testing, medical marijuana, and off-duty conduct. Idaho voters will decide whether that path remains available. Houston: Changing Enforcement Without Legalization Houston voters will consider another approach to marijuana policy: making enforcement of certain marijuana offenses a lower priority for local police. Proposition A would make enforcement of Class A and Class B misdemeanor marijuana possession the Houston Police Department’s lowest law enforcement priority. It would also establish reporting requirements and prohibit no-knock search warrants by Houston police officers. Marijuana possession would remain illegal under Texas law. Texas does have a limited medical cannabis program. Its Compassionate Use Program allows qualifying patients to obtain prescribed low-THC cannabis for certain medical conditions. The state expanded that program in 2025, but Houston’s proposal wouldn’t change it. For employers, the most relevant consideration may be criminal background screening. If police make marijuana possession a lower enforcement priority, fewer arrests and prosecutions could follow. Over time, that could influence the marijuana-related records employers encounter when screening applicants. But Proposition A wouldn’t erase existing convictions or change the legal standards governing employment decisions based on criminal history. Employers would still need to follow applicable federal, state, and local requirements, including the Fair Credit Reporting Act when obtaining employment background reports from consumer reporting agencies. Houston’s proposal illustrates how marijuana policy can change at the local level, even when the underlying state criminal law remains the same. What Happens After Election Day? Massachusetts could eliminate recreational sales while preserving medical marijuana accommodations. Idaho could restrict future citizen-led legalization efforts without changing its drug-testing laws. Houston could reduce enforcement priorities without legalizing marijuana. Medical marijuana protections may continue even when recreational laws change. A positive drug test may indicate prior exposure without necessarily establishing current impairment. And changes in criminal enforcement may influence background screening without changing the laws governing employment decisions. Federal requirements also remain important, particularly for employees in safety-sensitive positions subject to Department of Transportation drug-testing rules. As results come in, employers should focus on what changes, when those changes take effect, and whether existing workplace policies need attention. Voters will decide what direction marijuana policy takes next. Employers will have to navigate what those decisions mean in the workplace . This article was originally published on Forbes.com This article originally appeared on Forbes at https://www.forbes.com/sites/alonzomartinez/2026/10/12/marijuana-is-on-the-ballot-in-2026-the-debate-has-changed/

item.title: Despite pushback from both parties, Trump defends his diesel deal with Russia
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
By Steve Holland WASHINGTON, Oct 12 (Reuters) - President Donald Trump on Monday defended a diesel oil deal he made with Russia as lawmakers from both parties complained the agreement appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian energy until Moscow ‌ends its aggression against Ukraine. Trump has said the deal to lift sanctions on Russian oil exports would help bring down high fuel ‌prices. However some analysts doubted the amount of diesel Trump has said Russia would provide over the next three months would do much to bring down prices, since it ​is equal to about 12 hours of global consumption of the fuel. On Friday, Trump said Russia had agreed to supply diesel to global markets, and his administration temporarily lifted US sanctions on Russian fuel designed to deprive Moscow of revenue for its war on Ukraine. On Monday, Trump said the deal would help American farmers and ranchers. The price of diesel has surged more than 60% since Trump launched a war against Iran seven months ago, and high prices ‌have jeopardized Republican chances to maintain thin majorities ⁠in the US Congress in the November 3 midterm elections. On Sunday a group of Republican and Democratic US senators called on Trump to "reverse course" on the diesel supply deal with Russia. They said his deal may violate a ⁠2022 law designed to support Ukraine in its bid to repel Russian invaders. "We should be tightening sanctions further, not undercutting them by allowing the import of Russian diesel and risking erasing our leverage, damaging our credibility with allies, and emboldening our adversaries," said Republican Senator Jerry Moran in a social media post. Trump has ​blamed ​Ukraine's attacks on Russian oil refineries as a leading factor for higher diesel ​prices. "I made the right choice for the American People — ALWAYS, ‌AMERICA FIRST! President DONALD J. TRUMP," Trump said in a social media post. On Monday, Trump rejected criticism of the deal from members of his own party, in comments to reporters as he departed the White House on a trip to Ohio. "Well, I think these are Republicans that can't really be serious," he said. "We can do a restriction on oil, but the rest of the world would be greatly, greatly affected if we do that." Trump and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy bickered over the weekend about the Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries. Trump said Ukraine needs a new president ‌and Zelenskiy promised to hold elections if Russia would agree to a 60-day ceasefire. Trump ​on Sunday declared that Russia and Ukraine agreed to halt attacks on each other's energy ​infrastructure. Whether such a deal will hold was unclear. "Well, they agreed," ​Trump told reporters. "They agreed because I said they agreed. ... That war has to be over with." Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov ‌said contacts were proceeding about a possible energy ceasefire ​as announced by Trump. He declined to ​comment on whether the ceasefire would apply only to oil refineries. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy said Kyiv favoured a ceasefire, but both sides had to observe it. He said it was "increasingly clear" that Russia was unwilling to accept it as Moscow hit six Ukrainian energy ​facilities on Monday Zelenskiy told Fox News' "America's Newsroom" program ‌on Monday that Ukraine's attacks on Russian refineries were not the leading cause of rising fuel prices. "Everybody understands that the prices on ​diesel — it doesn't depend on our attacks on diesel in Russia. Everybody understands that it depends on the blocking... the ​Strait of Hormuz," he said. (Reporting By Steve Holland; Editing by David Gregorio) This article originally appeared on Reuters at https://www.yahoo.com/news/articles/trump-defends-russia-diesel-deal-152736373.html

item.title: Trump said Russia agreed to an energy ceasefire. Attacks on Ukraine's power grid continued.
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Emergency services responded to a Russian drone strike on a residential building in Kharkiv, north-eastern Ukraine on Monday [EPA] Russia struck six Ukrainian energy facilities hours after US President Donald Trump announced the two countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, Volodymyr Zelensky has said. Despite Trump stating on Sunday the truce would be "effective immediately", the Ukrainian president said Russia had hit "our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities". There were blackouts in the city of Izyum after a Russian strike destroyed power grids, Ukraine's state news agency Ukrinform said, while energy and railway infrastructure in western Ukraine was also targeted overnight. On Monday, Russia's Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said Ukraine does not deserve the "respite" a ceasefire would bring. What's behind Trump's energy ceasefire claim? Zelensky backs Trump's 'energy ceasefire' but says Russia continues to hit power plants Zelensky said 33 people had been injured in the strikes on energy facilities across the country. He told Fox News: "We did not attack, while Russia attacked our gas stations, energy infrastructure, and other facilities." "I think it was Putin's answer to President Trump," he added. Global conflicts have pushed fuel prices higher ahead of the US midterm elections and on Friday Trump announced a plan to import Russian diesel into the US on Friday. On Monday, Ukraine's state-owned grid operator Ukrenergo reported "new power cuts" in Kharkiv, Donetsk and Zaporizhzhia due to damage caused to energy equipment by Russian attacks. Electricity rationing has been introduced in parts of Ukraine to avoid overloading damaged equipment, Ukrenergo said. Zelensky said on X the strikes were proof Russia was "unwilling to accept an energy ceasefire". On Monday evening, Kyiv's mayor Vitali Klitschko posted on Telegram that a drone hit a 25-story residential building in the Darnytskyi district. Several cars in the building's courtyard were also on fire, he said, with one person dead and 11 injured. Watch: What could Trump's energy ceasefire claim mean for Ukraine? When Trump first announced the ceasefire on Sunday , Zelensky said it was "news to him" that a truce was in effect, but he backed the proposed ceasefire as a "major step toward ending the war, if the Americans truly step in now and make sure Russians respect the energy ceasefire". Asked about the ceasefire on Monday, Trump said they agreed "because I said you agree", adding that the war "has to get settled". "That war is a disaster if you see the numbers," he said. For months, Ukraine and Russia have been exchanging strikes on energy infrastructure , disrupting energy supplies on both sides. Moscow has said the installations it hits are legitimate targets as they support Ukraine's military operation, while Zelensky has characterised Ukrainian attacks deep inside Russian territory as part of an effort to "reduce Russia's ability to finance the war". Analysis by BBC Verify on both Ukrainian and Russian strikes during the war have found both sides have increased their attacks in the lead up to the next winter. In 2026, BBC Verify has recorded 273 strikes on Russian-controlled oil and gas facilities, more than double the 124 recorded over the same period in 2025. Separately, analysis of data aggregated by global conflict monitor, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data project (Acled), recorded 2.4 times as many reported Russian attacks affecting Ukraine's energy network so far this year. Energy facilities in Kharkiv were hit by Russian strikes on Sunday evening, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said [EPA/Shutterstock] Trump has been urging Ukraine to stop strikes on Russian oil infrastructure, so Russia can fulfil the recently struck deal to release diesel to the US and the global market. The deal temporarily undoes US sanctions on energy imports, which Zelensky described as a "gift" to Russian President Vladimir Putin. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Britain "strongly supports President Trump's call today for a sustained energy ceasefire to start now", while France, Canada and the EU also expressed support. However, there has been a mixed response among European officials. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the bloc would welcome an energy ceasefire "when it holds". Kallas said at a meeting of EU foreign ministers on Monday: "We haven't yet seen that also Russia will stick to it." Meanwhile, Estonia's foreign minister said the ceasefire was "not working". item.title: What needs to happen for Democrats or Republicans to win control of the House
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
It's crunch time. With less than a month to go until the 2026 midterm elections, Democratic and Republican candidates for the U.S. House of Representatives nationwide are making one last push to persuade voters in their districts — and help their party win or retain control of the chamber on Nov. 3. The stakes are high. President Trump has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block parts of the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again) . Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. (The average number lost since World War II? Twenty-six .) Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses seats across a wide range of competitive districts — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election. But the past doesn't necessarily predict the future, and Republicans have certain advantages today that they didn't have before. Here's what needs to happen for each party to come out on top. Yahoo The races to watch The first thing to know about any House election is that while all 435 congressional districts are technically up for grabs, roughly 83% of those contests (representing about 360 seats) are not considered competitive. House incumbents have always had huge advantages: money and name recognition, mostly. But their head start has only widened in recent years as partisan polarization and redistricting have helped make the vast majority of congressional districts "safe" for one party . These days, incumbents tend to focus more on fending off primary challengers. The general election can be a breeze in comparison. As a result, this year's true battleground is relatively small. According to the nonpartisan Cook Political Report's " race ratings ," just 21 contests are genuine "tossups" at this point. Another 12 "lean Democratic," and 9 "lean Republican." There's also a third competitive category that includes 16 seats where Democrats are the "likely" winners, and 18 seats where the same could be said about Republicans. That's 76 competitive districts — again, out of 435. It's clear from looking at this year's ratings which party is playing more defense and which is playing more offense — and where. Six Democratic seats are too close to call; two more lean Republican; another three are likely to break for the GOP; and three are rated solidly Republican. That's a total of 14 potential blue-to-red flips for Democrats to worry about. Republicans, by contrast, have to worry about 25 red-to-blue flips — including a full 15 in the tossup category. Geographically, this year's tossups are concentrated in certain kinds of places: Rust Belt districts in states that have swung from party to party in the past (such as Michigan, Pennsylvania and Ohio); Mid-Atlantic suburbs (in states such as New York, Virginia and North Carolina) where Trump has scrambled some of the usual coalitions; and Sun Belt districts (think Florida, Texas, California and Nevada) where Latinos factor heavily. Trump carried many of these areas in 2024 . Overall, the map gives Democrats more pickup options — which could mean more paths to a House majority. The path to a Democratic House Senate and governor contests can be quirky — more state-specific and personality-driven. But national dynamics tend to play a larger role in shaping the composition of the incoming House. So it's not just a matter of who has more targets on the board. It's that the board itself tends to tilt to one side or the other, taking most of those targets with it. A recent example was the 2010 midterm election, when impatience with America's slow recovery from the 2008 financial collapse and frustration with President Barack Obama's response helped Republicans gain 64 House seats. Beyond the history of midterm backlash against the president's party, Democrats have two big advantages right now. One is that the current Republican majority is so minuscule — just 219 votes to 214, including an independent who caucuses with Republicans — that Democrats only need a net gain of three seats to win back the House. The other is that the board seems to be tilting in Democrats' favor — assuming the polls are right. Surveys suggest there's one underlying factor pulling the national electorate to the left: dissatisfaction with Trump. According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 60% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job compared with 37% who approve. That puts the president's net disapproval rating at about 23 percentage points. Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top issue this year: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today — as tariffs and the Iran war help drive prices up — 72% disapprove and 24% approve . That's a 48-point gap. President Trump arrives to speak at a campaign rally at F&M Bank Arena on Oct. 10, 2026, in Clarksville, Tenn. AP Photo/Alex Brandon Democrats aren't particularly popular. But for the party in power, it may be hard to overcome this level of dissatisfaction with the status quo. That's why, when pollsters ask their so-called generic ballot question — If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? — Americans are currently giving Democrats a substantial lead of about 9 percentage points , on average. Making matters worse for Republicans, that lead has grown over the last month as some voters who favored Trump in 2024 — including some Latinos and independents — say they're planning to vote Democratic. Over the last two weeks, Cook has shifted 33 of its race ratings toward the Democrats as well. To put a 9-point lead in perspective, Democrats were leading by an average of 7 points on the generic ballot at this point in 2018, with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate. Four weeks later, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House. If the polls are right, Democrats might win control of the House again. The path to a Republican House But are the polls right? In recent days, Republicans have pointed to some surprising survey results on the Senate side — including Democratic leads in rural red states such as Iowa , Kansas and Nebraska — to argue that pollsters might be misjudging public sentiment. They're not wrong to say the polls have missed in the past. Polling errors are commonplace; they happen in most elections. But they tend to be random and to change directions from one cycle to another . The Trump era has been a little different. In each of the three presidential contests that Trump himself has competed in, the final average of polls conducted before Election Day underestimated Republicans' performance in the popular vote by an average of 3.8 percentage points, according to data journalist Nate Silver . The theory is that a phenomenon called nonresponse bias — in which Democratic voters are more eager or available to respond to pollsters than Republican voters — might have made Democratic support look stronger than it actually was. Pollsters try to adjust for this by weighting their results — that is, using statistical methods to give less weight to respondents who are overrepresented demographically and more weight to respondents who are underrepresented demographically. But it's difficult to predict in advance who will show up on Election Day. This time around, there are signs that rural Republicans are not responding to pollsters in certain states . Could that mean Republican candidates in those places will outperform their polling? Possibly. But experts say it may also mean that rural Republicans are less supportive of the GOP than they were in 2024 — potentially voting Democratic or staying home on Nov. 3. A voter walks toward his polling place. REUTERS / REUTERS After all, there's been virtually no polling bias toward Democrats in Trump era elections when Trump himself wasn't on the ballot. In fact, the polls since 2016 have overestimated Republican support in midterm elections (by an average of 0.2%) and off-year, special and runoff elections (by an average of 1.3%), according to Silver . Either way, pollsters aren't seeing signs of this rural effect in most states — and even if they were, it might make only a minor dent in Democrats' 9-point national lead . Redistricting is the other Republican advantage. House redistricting efforts typically take place every 10 years, after each new census reveals changes in population distribution. But last summer, Trump successfully pushed GOP legislators in Texas to pass new congressional district boundaries five years earlier than normal to help Republicans win five additional House seats in 2026. This kicked off a tit-for-tat cycle that saw nine states adopt new congressional maps for the midterms — some to benefit Democrats, others Republicans. Now that the dust has settled, Cook projects that Republicans could win nine seats because of redistricting (in Alabama, Florida, Louisiana, North Carolina, Ohio, Tennessee and Texas), while Democrats could win five (in California and Utah). That would net the GOP four seats overall. It's not what Republicans initially hoped to gain from gerrymandering. "We're not gonna win all 13 of those redistricted seats. That's correct. We're not," GOP House Majority Whip Tom Emmer of Minnesota told Axios recently . But it's also not nothing. The hope for the GOP is that some combination of polling error and redistricting boost — along with a late influx of hundreds of millions of dollars to help defend districts Trump won in 2024 — will be just enough to preserve their slim House majority. item.title: Some ranchers question Trump’s policies as industry faces rising costs
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Rancher Yvette Mannon was already dealing with a destructive wildfire and rising fuel costs before the US announced new foreign beef imports [Yvette Mannon] Nebraska rancher Yvette Mannon was already having a rough year. In April, a wildfire destroyed 1,600 grazing acres and 13 miles (21 km) of fence along the ranch she bought in 2002. The ranch is nestled in a corner of Nebraska that's home to rolling green hills under sweeping Midwestern skies, the landscape dotted with grain silos and feedlots alongside fields and fields of bovines. Mannon's 300 cattle survived the blaze - but the fencing needed to be replaced, and the herd still needed to be fed. With steel prices at their highest levels in years, heavily affected by tariffs imposed by US President Donald Trump, that meant spending $4.89 a foot - for a total exceeding $300,000. On top of that, because so much good grazing land had been destroyed, Mannon also needed a tractor out every day delivering hay to her cattle - at a time when diesel prices, spiking due to the Iran War, were up more than 40% from the previous year. Then in August, the Trump administration announced it would import 300,000 metric tons of duty-free foreign beef in a bid to lower consumer prices. The news hit right before the September-November window when most US calves are weaned and sold. The cattle market tanked immediately. 'It felt like a betrayal' "So we're 'Buy American', 'Let's Make America Great'," said Mannon, 63, who voted for Trump. "But for you guys over here, sorry." "It just felt like a betrayal," she said. Many farmers and ranchers across the US say they are being hit from all sides. Recent years have been difficult, with drought affecting crops and already historically low cattle herds. But they say government policies have added to the strain. That has left some in Nebraska, which overwhelmingly backed President Trump during the last election, reassessing their political allegiances. Dan Osborn, an independent candidate running against Trump-backed Republican Pete Ricketts, is performing surprisingly well in the polls ahead of November's Senate race. Republicans seem keenly aware of the discord and frustration among farmers. Both Trump and Nebraska Governor Jim Pillen have in recent weeks announced relief policies aimed at lowering fuel costs for farmers and ranchers, who say they have been struggling for months. Cattle farming is big business in Nebraska - where ranchers say they are facing soaring costs [Getty Images] The Iran War has sent diesel and fertiliser prices skyrocketing - both daily necessities for agricultural operations. Tariffs have affected machinery costs and repairs, as well as steel and lumber prices. And decisions by the Trump administration - whether it be importing foreign beef or opening up the southern border to Mexican cattle - have sent already-volatile markets into overdrive. Many producers are losing hundreds of dollars per head of cattle. "All of this hit cattle markets, as a whole, negatively," said James Mitchell, an assistant professor and agricultural economist at the University of Arkansas. Cattle markets run in 10-12 year cycles, he said, with some good years and some bad. The industry recently enjoyed a particularly lucrative period, where low supply and high demand drove up prices. But now, the market is clearly on a downswing. Jake Wolfinger, 45, has been weathering the downturn at his feedlot near Lexington, Nebraska. He and his wife are both Ohio natives hailing from multi-generational farming families. They moved to Nebraska - which enjoys lush land and the most groundwater in the nation - to strike out on their own. Jake Wolfinger, 45, says he is frustrated with the way Trump has intervened in the beef market [BBC/Lori Potter] The Wolfingers bought a dilapidated feedlot in 2010, which they have turned into a sophisticated operation with 5,500 cattle. Neighbours point to them as an example of what hard work can still do in a tough industry. But Wolfinger did not factor the Iran War, tariffs or foreign beef imports into his planning. "Things were just chumming along pretty good," he said, selling cattle for $240 per hundredweight - but that's dropped to $225. That may not seem like much, but it means a loss of potentially hundreds of dollars a head. Wolfinger is also contending with sky-high diesel costs, with some equipment going through 400-gallon tanks a day. "It really makes a guy think," he said. A Trump supporter, Wolfinger said he voted for the president because "we needed his spirit in this country". He also expressed frustration with what he called "woke DEI" policies on the left. But he is unhappy with the way the president has intervened in the beef market. "People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business, because it's harvest time," Wolfinger said. 'People need to stay the hell out of farmers' business' Forty miles northwest, near Callaway, Nebraska, 54-year-old Duane Kimball stands in his shed surrounded by machinery - and a huge Trump banner along one wall. "The daily upcharge… is kind of painful," he said. "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit." Kimball believed the Iran War would have ended long ago. But he does not blame Trump for all of his economic challenges. "To pin that on this administration, I don't think is a fair assessment," he said. He pointed to cumbersome regulations as well as the rising cost of machinery and fertiliser - trends that began before Trump returned to the White House. "I know a lot of people have had to go back to their banks and increase their lines of credit," said Duane Kimball [BBC/Lori Potter] Mannon, who returned to her native Nebraska and bought the ranch after a career in banking, believes the agricultural industry will show its feelings at the midterms. But like many around here, she prefers not to engage in too much political debate. That is not a problem for her friend and nearby rancher Jim Jenkins. A former independent senatorial candidate, Jenkins is fiercely proud of Nebraska agriculture and his own ranch, which is on land his family homesteaded more than 150 years ago. Jenkins has been so incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry that he wrote an opinion article over the summer in an Omaha paper. He has felt the squeeze personally too, citing high diesel, fertiliser, lumber and steel costs - everything from barbed wire to fence posts. That has been compounded by "uncertainty" over what may happen next, he said, and what the next Trump announcement might mean for the industry. "Those are the things that keep you up at night," the 69-year-old told BBC News. An outspoken Trump critic who didn't vote for the president during any of his White House bids, Jenkins knows he is an outlier among his conservative neighbours. When Trump was first elected, Jenkins said he hoped he would turn out "to be a practical business guy". Now, he said, "I think he's been anything but practical". Jim Jenkins says he is incensed by the policies he feels are harming Nebraska's agricultural industry [BBC] But for many Trump-supporting farmers and ranchers, the president's decisions - even when they hit them economically - deserve the benefit of the doubt. "We've all known this about Trump. He just kind of could be a little 'shoot, fire, aim,'" Wolfinger said. "I wish you could, you know, put the gun back and holster it and then think about it." But, he said, "I think he's, for the most part, trying to run this country in the right direction". [BBC] What are the US midterms? A simple guide The Republican candidates walking a Trump tightrope Don Cantrell, whose grandfather started farming family land that now stretches to 12,000 acres, said he is still getting hit on diesel and admits the president "does some stupid things" and "says some stupid things". But Cantrell believes Trump has been the "best president overall". His establishment of DOGE - the Department of Government Efficiency - for example, was exactly what he felt the country needed. "Let's cut government waste," he said. "There's so much waste." Don Cantrell says he believes Trump has been the "best president overall" - citing his efforts to "cut government waste" [BBC] Trump also maintains stances on social issues - like abortion and praising Christianity - that align with many Nebraskan voters' personal convictions. "I think, in general, if you're conservative in this country, you're going to vote conservative," Wolfinger said. Don Batie, 67, agrees: "There's a lot of other issues besides agriculture." Still, the economic realities are hard to ignore, he said. Batie retired from farming last year for a combination of personal and economic reasons. The corn and soybean farmer watched as prices fell from $7 a bushel for corn in early 2022 to just $4.29 three years later. But costs have not gone down, he said, with tariffs and inflation contributing to his bottom line. As a result, he has had to abandon his longtime dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter. Don Batie, 67, says he has had to abandon his dream of passing on the 400-acre farm he owns to his daughter [BBC] "It just wasn't going to work now," he said, sitting at the dining room table in the home he grew up in. He only came to that realisation within the past year after crunching the numbers. "I knew things hadn't been good," he said. "But when I started working on the numbers… I was like, 'This is going to be bad.'" Batie voted for Trump in 2016 and again in the primary - but not in 2024, because he was disappointed with his policies. He said he had heard similar dissatisfaction throughout the state. "They're still strong Republicans," he said of those people."But they're not a Trump supporter anymore." Cattle still need to be bought and sold, and vast ranches - many multi-generational - operate throughout the state [Lori Potter] All over Nebraska, however, the industry soldiers on. On a rainy Thursday in Broken Bow, buyers clad in cowboy hats, plaid shirts and denim gathered for the regular indoor cattle auction. Calves still need to be bought and sold, and ranch operations - many multi-generational - do not pause for politics. Across the train tracks, past feed and hardware stores, Yvette Mannon summed up Nebraskans' resilience and fortitude. "People in agriculture are eternal optimists," she said "Otherwise we wouldn't get in it." item.title: Trump says he's 'looking at' firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as U.S. ambassador to Greece
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Donald Trump answered he's "looking at" firing Kimberly Guilfoyle when asked about the embattled U.S. ambassador to Greece on Monday. Trump told reporters as he left the White House for a campaign rally that his administration is "looking at it" and added that it's "not happy" over reports alleging that she used her official position and links to the Trump family to get money from a donor . A Trump donor told ABC News last week that Guilfoyle offered access to top Trump officials in exchange for cash. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: Kimberly Guilfoyle, President Trump's nominee to be the US ambassador to Greece, speaks alongside President Donald Trump, during a Greek Independence Day celebration in the East Room of the White House in Washington, March 24, 2025. Eric Deters, a former lawyer, conservative media personality and Trump donor, alleged that Guilfoyle asked him to pay her $100,000 credit card bill in July 2025 -- days before her Senate confirmation hearing. Trump donor accuses Kimberly Guilfoyle of asking him to pay her $100K credit card bill: 'It was all quid pro quo' "It was all quid pro quo," Deters claimed about the request from Guilfoyle, who is the former wife of California Gov. Gavin Newsom and ex-fiance of Donald Trump Jr. The Wall Street Journal first reported on Deters' accusations. Deters provided messages to ABC News he says he exchanged with Guilfoyle on the subject. In one message from that period, Deters alleges Guilfoyle wrote, "Honey please I need you to get this done for me today," which Deters alleged was in reference to the desired credit card payment. ABC News has reached out to Guilfoyle, her attorney and the U.S. Embassy in Greece for comment and have not heard back. In a statement released late Sunday, Guilfoyle's lawyers claimed that the money she was seeking was for appearances and speaking engagements that predate her nomination that have not been paid, according to The Associated Press. Deters denies he owed Guilfoyle any money. He said he ended up not making the payment because he didn’t have the money. Deters is considered a controversial character in Kentucky politics. He ran for Kentucky governor in 2023 and to represent Kentucky's 4th Congressional District in the House in 2024; he lost both races in the primaries. A former lawyer, Deters had his law license suspended in 2012 for actions in multiple cases including comments he made about a judge and improper solicitation of a possible client. In refusing to reinstate Deters' law license in 2021, the Kentucky Supreme Court said he had a "notorious propensity" for filing "malicious or frivolous lawsuits," according to court documents. Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images - PHOTO: President Donald Trump speaks with reporters before walking to board Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House, Oct. 12, 2026, in Washington. In a statement to the Wall Street Journal, the U.S. embassy in Greece said Guilfoyle's "career in and out of public service is guided by deep and abiding values" and "the Ambassador remains committed to representing the American people with dedication and integrity." Secretary of State Marco Rubio said he wouldn't answer questions about Guilfoyle's alleged conduct last week while departing Athens, Greece. "I don't even know if it's true or not true," Rubio said. "So it's just not going to work that way, and it will certainly not going to work that way when I'm sitting in another country." But White House and State Department leadership have held discussions on how to address the allegations against Guilfoyle, including possibly dismissing her, according to two sources familiar with the matter. Both sources cautioned, however, that no final decision had been made; one source said the the president would have final say over any action. Several officials close to Rubio have expressed their frustration with Guilfoyle, whose reported misconduct loomed over Rubio’s high-profile visit to Athens last week. Guilfoyle was present throughout the secretary’s program in Greece, even appearing at some events that she had not been invited by the State Department to attend, one U.S. official said. The official said that the State Department’s inspector general is examining claims of possible misconduct by Guilfoyle, but it is unclear if a formal probe has been launched and the department has declined to publicly comment on any investigation. ABC News' Jay O'Brien contributed to this report. This article originally appeared on ABC News at https://abcnews.com/Politics/trump-firing-us-ambassador-greece-kimberly-guilfoyle/story?id=137209661

item.title: Selma Blair appears emotional in court as lawyer explains what led to flight altercation
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NEW YORK (AP) — Actor Selma Blair was arrested after she was accused of injuring two flight attendants on a trip from Los Angeles to New York. She was also accused of kicking a police officer taking her to the hospital and kicking a nurse once she got there. She pleaded not guilty Monday night to two counts of assault for state charges involving the officer and the nurse. And she faces separate federal charges based on what happened on the flight, which her representatives say was brought on by a severe medical emergency. Blair, 54, was detained by police at around 11 p.m. Sunday after the Delta Air Lines jet parked at the gate at John F. Kennedy International Airport, the Port Authority of New York and New Jersey said in a statement. Blair and one of the flight attendants were taken to a hospital for evaluation, the Port Authority said. A police officer taking her to Jamaica Hospital Medical Center said in charging documents that while she was securing Blair to a stretcher, Blair pulled a leg from the straps and kicked her repeatedly around the face, neck and chest, causing serious pain and substantial swelling. Later, a nurse moving Blair said the actor kicked her in the chest, causing substantial pain. She was arraigned on two counts of second-degree assault late Monday at a court in Queens, where her lawyer entered a not guilty plea on her behalf. She appeared to cry as she stood in court in handcuffs, wearing jeans and a white hooded sweatshirt. Her attorney Shawn Barnes told a judge her actions were not intentional. He said the actor, who has multiple sclerosis, missed several doses of “a powerful medication that controls severe neurological symptoms,” according to the New York Daily News and New York Post. He said she had gotten on the flight in Los Angeles after a heavy workload, and hit her head during the flight. He said these factors along with the altitude led to “a state of severe confusion and disorientation.” The judge set her bail at $20,000 cash or $60,000 bond and set the next hearing for January. She left court with her lawyers. Details of what happened aboard the aircraft weren’t immediately disclosed by the airline, police or the FBI, which was investigating, but Delta said in a statement it “has zero tolerance for unruly or unlawful behavior, as the safety of our customers and crew always comes first.” In air traffic communications, the Delta pilot asked the tower to have medical personnel waiting at the gate to treat bite marks and a bloody nose, but said ambulances were not necessary. “It sounds like the disruptive passenger also bashed her head on the bulkhead or something like that,” the pilot told the tower, according to audio posted on the ATC app. “So we’ll obviously have to get her potentially checked out as well as involved with law enforcement.” The FBI also issued Blair a notice charging her with assault related to her actions aboard the aircraft, according to a federal law enforcement official who spoke to The Associated Press on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak publicly about the matter. Those charges will be handled through the petty violations court in federal court in Brooklyn. No date has been set for Blair’s appearance. It's not the first time Blair has had issues aboard a plane. In 2016, Blair apologized for making statements she later regretted during a flight from Cancun to Los Angeles. She said she had mixed alcohol with medication, causing her to black out. Blair had major roles in films including 1999's “Cruel Intentions,” 2001's “Legally Blonde” and 2004's “Hellboy.” In recent years, she has advocated for disability rights after getting her multiple sclerosis diagnosis in 2018 . In 2023, she joined President Joe Biden at the White House to celebrate the anniversary of the Americans with Disabilities Act. ___ Yamat reported from Las Vegas and Dalton from Los Angeles. AP Transportation Writer Josh Funk contributed to this report. item.title: Sean 'Diddy' Combs reportedly leaves prison briefly after suffering head injury
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
Sean “Diddy” Combs was transported from federal prison for medical treatment early Saturday after suffering a head injury, according to TMZ, while his representative told Newsweek that Combs’ team was working to confirm the situation. “We are aware of the reports concerning Sean Combs and are working to confirm the circumstances. Sean’s health and well-being are our immediate concern, and we appreciate everyone who has reached out,” the representative said Monday. Sources at FCI Fort Dix in New Jersey told TMZ that an ambulance carrying Combs left the prison grounds around 1 a.m. The outlet said it was unclear how Combs sustained the injury and that it had not confirmed whether he was taken to a hospital. Combs was conscious and speaking when he was returned to the prison before sunrise, TMZ said. The Federal Bureau of Prisons declined to discuss Combs’ medical status with Newsweek . “For privacy, safety, and security reasons, we do not comment on the conditions of confinement for any incarcerated individual, including quarters assignment or medical status,” the agency said in an email. The reported medical incident follows shortly after an NBC News investigation into Combs’ life at Fort Dix, citing four men who spent time in his unit, along with photos and videos the outlet reviewed. NBC reported allegations that Combs had access to contraband cellphones and alcohol and paid other inmates to perform tasks for him. Sean “Diddy” Combs arrives at the Billboard Music Awards in Las Vegas, on May 15, 2022. Combs’ spokesperson downplayed the report, while the Bureau of Prisons declined to comment on his conditions. NBC subsequently reported that Combs was placed in solitary confinement following publication of the story. Combs had previously been placed in solitary confinement following a fight with another inmate over the summer, NBC News reported in July. What Did Sean ‘Diddy’ Combs Do? Combs was found guilty in 2025 of transporting two women, identified in court as Cassie Ventura and “Jane,” for the purpose of prostitution, violations of the Mann Act. He was acquitted of the more serious racketeering conspiracy and sex-trafficking charges. The split verdict followed a closely watched federal trial in Manhattan. Prosecutors had accused Combs of operating a criminal enterprise and using his businesses and employees to facilitate sexual encounters, allegations that formed part of the government’s broader racketeering case. The jury ultimately rejected the racketeering and sex-trafficking counts while convicting him on the two prostitution-related transportation charges. Combs was sentenced to 50 months in federal prison, a $500,000 fine, and five years of supervised release. He appealed his sentence to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit, arguing that the sentencing judge improperly relied on conduct connected to charges he had been acquitted of. The appeals court heard arguments on April 9, 2026, but did not immediately issue a ruling. Separately, Combs faces dozens of lawsuits alleging misconduct. Those cases are proceeding independently of his federal criminal appeal, meaning the outcome of his challenge to the prison sentence would not itself resolve the civil claims against him. Combs has a projected release date of March 2, 2028, according to Bureau of Prisons records. The date is subject to change and was recently pushed back from January 21, 2028. item.title: Trump's spree of new projects mirrors his run-up to the 2018 midterms
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
President Trump has been appearing around the US in the run-up to the midterm elections, announcing economic development projects — from a possible pipeline in Alaska to a steel plant in Iowa to an aluminum smelter in Oklahoma — that he says will transform the country. "In the real economy, we are blowing it away," he said at a weekend stop in Tennessee . Trump's message of confidence comes as the ultimate shape of these projects remains far from certain and often directly echoes his pitch at this stage in the 2018 midterm elections, a Yahoo Finance review found. That election eight years ago was the last time Trump faced midterm voters and also saw him tout projects — most notably a Foxconn electronics manufacturing plant planned for Wisconsin — that turned out to be less than advertised. President Trump shakes hands with then-Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker at a groundbreaking for a Foxconn plant on June 28, 2018, in Mount Pleasant, Wisc. (Brian Cassella/Chicago Tribune/Tribune News Service via Getty Images) Chicago Tribune via Getty Images "FoxConn … had a ribbon-cutting a few months ago," Trump said at a stop in Wisconsin on the eve of the 2018 election , pledging that the project was set to bring in "almost 15,000 jobs and there is no plant like it in the United States." But the company eventually scrapped much of its manufacturing plans at the site and shifted the focus to data centers. Today, it employs only a reported 1,200 people at the site. The president's penchant for promises is on display again as Election Day nears. On Tuesday, he is set to travel to Alaska to tout a proposed $50 billion gas pipeline between South Korea and Alaska that could help Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan fend off a Democratic challenge. Trump unveiled the project earlier this month in the Oval Office with Sullivan at his side, but South Korean officials immediately pushed back, saying no final investment decision has been made . Korean President Lee Jae Myung even added that the deal will only proceed once the project's "commercial viability is confirmed." President Trump listens to Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) during an announcement at the White House in September. (Kent Nishimura/AFP via Getty Images) KENT NISHIMURA via Getty Images Trump's promises in recent weeks have also included a $4 billion aluminum processing plant in Oklahoma . But local opposition to that plan — citing possible toxic chemicals and rising electricity prices — has led the town’s mayor and a board of trustees to pause zoning approvals, leaving the fate of the project up in the air. Even the project's developers recently reported to the SEC that "to complete this project, we will need to obtain substantial additional financing, and there can be no assurance that such financing will be available." That didn't slow Trump from saying earlier this month that it would be "the largest aluminum factory, perhaps in the world, and you're going to make a fortune with it, lots of jobs, a lot of everything." A record of Trump overstating his own role The 2018 campaign was also notable for Trump overstating his role in various projects. In 2018, Trump often mentioned Apple's plans to spend $350 billion in the US, which he said was happening "only" because of his tax cut. "We are making some of the biggest and most important deals in our country's history," Trump posted on his then-Twitter account at the time. Yet those claims were an inflation of Apple's investment promises — which totaled about $55 billion for 2018 — and the company said at the time that they were made not just for tax reasons. Apple has been adept at repackaging long-term investment promises for each administration, with overlapping pledges made during Trump's first term, the Biden administration, and then again as Trump returned to office. Apple chair Tim Cook, center, applauds as President Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping arrive for a state dinner at the White House on Sept. 24. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images) BRENDAN SMIALOWSKI via Getty Images Trump has also focused on a recent announcement of plans for a new $15 billion steel plant in Iowa. Iowa's governor recently signed a bill to move forward with government incentives, but the steel plant’s ultimate fate still raises questions, especially given that one of its financiers previously filed for Chapter 11 protection . Trump's track record stretching back to 2018 has drawn skepticism about those plans. Iowa's Democratic nominee for governor, Rob Sand, noted the benefits of a steel plant while also reportedly telling voters at one stop that they have reason to be skeptical of a promise "that gets rolled out right before an election." The example he pointed to? Foxconn. Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance. item.title: Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion after failed execution, 911 calls reveal
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
NASHVILLE, Tenn. (AP) — Emergency help for Christa Pike was delayed by confusion among first responders and Tennessee prison officials following her failed execution last month, according to 911 dispatch recordings. The recordings, obtained Monday by The Associated Press through a public records request, show that precious minutes elapsed as officials and responders tried to figure out whether a request for emergency help in the execution chamber was legitimate. The initial 911 call came in at 8:40 p.m. on Sept. 30, just over an hour after the attempted lethal injection got underway . But the caller was unable to provide a code that would help verify the legitimacy of the request. “Per supervisors here at the DEC (Department of Emergency Communications) we have been informed it is a false call,” a dispatcher says at 9:03 p.m. “There is no medical assistance needed at Riverbend Prison.” It wasn’t until about half an hour after the initial call — close to 9:11 p.m. — that prison officials affirmed it was real and began letting responders through the gates. Neither the Tennessee Department of Correction nor Pike’s legal team immediately responded to requests for comment. The prisoner becomes a patient Pike, 50, was hospitalized after surviving two doses of pentobarbital as the state tried to execute her for the 1995 stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. She was 18 when she tortured and killed Slemmer with her boyfriend, becoming one of the youngest women to be sentenced to death. State protocol calls for a second dose of pentobarbital if the first doesn’t result in death, but it doesn’t spell out what to do if an inmate survives the second injection. The first 911 call, released only as a written transcript, reported that Pike was unconscious and not breathing normally. After being taken to a hospital, Pike was on a ventilator for several days. At one point, her attorneys did not expect her to survive. She regained consciousness last Tuesday and began talking limitedly and walking with assistance, they said. Pike was discharged from the hospital and returned to the women’s prison where she was housed for 30 years, her lawyers said Saturday. Confusion begins with the initial 911 call The initial call came from a person whose name and title were redacted. The caller told a dispatcher that they were at the Riverbend Maximum Security Institution where they had tried to execute someone, but she was still alive. As emergency responders worked to verify the call, they were in touch with representatives of the prison’s Central Control, who said they “would have been the ones to call in" and they "did not make that call,” according to a recording time-stamped at 9:07 p.m. Around the same time, a first responder could be heard over the radio saying, “Somebody is outside the gate at the prison telling us that it’s real and demanding us to go in. They say they are some sort of state official. I need somebody to get out to the gate and talk to those people.” Central Control confirmed the call was legitimate a few minutes later, clearing the way for responders to enter through the gates at about 9:11 p.m. An AP reporter witnessed an ambulance and fire trucks pull up to the building inside the prison campus at 9:14 p.m. At 9:34 p.m., as medics were transporting Pike to a hospital, one asked dispatch to make sure the prison knew where they were taking her. "Just ’cause there’s been so much other confusion, I want to make sure they are aware of this,” the responder said. Two other calls were made The Nashville Department of Emergency Communications released with some redactions the batch of audio recordings from dispatchers. Police said the audio from the first 911 call was exempt from public disclosure under state law. Two subsequent emergency calls were made, including one at 9:08 p.m. by one of Pike’s attorneys, Kelly Gleason. “My client, Christa Gail Pike, is undergoing a state execution. She has completed the stages of the protocol and last we knew from the attorney who is present, she is still alive and breathing and needs immediate life-saving care,” Gleason said on the call. Further executions paused pending review The Tennessee Department of Correction has not said what went wrong in the attempted execution. Gov. Bill Lee paused further execution attempts pending a review. It’s unclear whether the state will try executing Pike again. Medical experts have raised a few possibilities that could explain how Pike was able to survive, including potential drug quality issues and the placement of IV lines causing the drug to pool in her tissue. Before the execution attempt, Pike’s attorneys told courts and prison officials that she had a blood disorder that could cause clotting at injection sites. ___ Johnson reported from Seattle and Schoenbaum from Salt Lake City. item.title: Victims and suspected shooter ID'd in Erie mass shooting as officials search for motive
item.description:
Source: Yahoo Top Stories (World)
ERIE, PA – Authorities identified the adult victims and the suspected gunman who were found dead after what police described as a "horrific" mass shooting at a home near Lake Erie. Police say on Oct. 9, a gunman fatally shot eight people, most of them relatives, including two young children and a pregnant woman. Authorities say the suspected shooter took his own life before police arrived. The victims included the suspect's wife, children and grandchildren, according to officials. Erie County Coroner Lyell Cook on Oct. 12 identified the adult victims as Twila Tanner, 51; Angelina Stone, 24, who was eight months pregnant; Jonathan Stone, 19; Matthew Stone Jr., 21; Michelle Stone, 44; and Lora Roberts, 37, reported the Erie Times-News, part of the USA TODAY Network . Cook identified the suspect as Matthew Stone Sr., 45. Cook told the Erie Times-News he is not permitted to release the names of the other two shooting victims, a 5-year-old boy and a girl who was 22 months old, because they are under 18. Erie police also did not release the names of the children. Erie Police Chief Rick Lorah said the suspect shot and killed six people inside the house on the evening of Oct. 9. The gunman then allegedly met two other women, including a family friend, outside the home after they arrived in a "state of distress," Lorah said, citing surveillance video. The gunman allegedly shot the two women before he reentered the home and shot himself, according to the police chief. Authorities have not determined a motive for the incident, which police are treating as a domestic situation because many of the victims are related and lived in the same home. Cook ruled the death of Matthew Stone Sr. as a suicide and the deaths of the others as homicides. All but Lora Roberts were pronounced dead at the scene, according to Cook. All members of the Stone family, as well as the two young children, lived at the home where the shooting occurred. Police said the suspect was married to Michelle Stone. Matthew Stone Jr., Jonathan Stone and Angelina Stone were their children, according to Erie police. The 5-year-old boy and the 22-month-old girl were Angelina Stone's children, police said. No autopsies were performed on any of the victims or the suspect. Lorah said officers recovered a handgun that was legally registered to the suspect. He said the suspected shooter last interacted with police in 2022 but did not provide any further information. "I think mental health is at play here, but I think it is too soon to really go into a motive," Lorah said. He said the crime scene was the "worst" he had ever seen in his many years working in law enforcement. "It was horrific," he said. Contributing: Trevor Hughes, USA TODAY; Ed Palattella, Erie Times-News Suicide Lifeline: If you or someone you know may be struggling with suicidal thoughts, you can call the U.S. National Suicide Prevention Lifeline at 988 any time, day or night, or chat online. Crisis Text Line provides free, 24/7, confidential support via text message to people in crisis when they text "HOME" to 741741.
